q: A student at a private university is disciplined for a campus speech criticizing the university's president. The university has no free-speech policy. The student sues, claiming a First Amendment violation. What is the strongest response?
o: The First Amendment applies only to Congress, so neither a private nor a state university can be sued.
The First Amendment binds only government actors, so a private university's discipline raises no First Amendment claim.
The speech is protected because criticism of officials is core political speech wherever it occurs.
The claim fails only because speech on a campus is unprotected unless the school designates a forum.
e: Rule: The First Amendment restricts only government action; it applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment and does not bind private actors.
oe: Too narrow. Through the Fourteenth Amendment, the First Amendment binds state and local governments too (Cantwell for Free Exercise).

Correct. The Fourteenth Amendment incorporates the First Amendment against state and local governments, but private actors aren't bound. Many private universities adopt free-speech policies voluntarily; this one didn't.
The value of the speech doesn't matter if there is no government action. The president of a private university is not a government official.
Campus speech isn't categorically unprotected, and forum doctrine applies to government property. The real problem is the lack of state action.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment overview — Big picture · incorporation and state action

q: Which statement best captures the holding and reasoning of West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette?
o: The state may teach civics and explain the flag salute, but it may not compel students to declare a belief, and secular objectors are protected too.
The state may require the salute of all students except those whose sincere religious beliefs forbid it, who must receive an exemption.
The state may require the salute only if it survives rational-basis review, which West Virginia's law failed for lack of evidence.
The state may not mention the flag or the Pledge in public schools, because any patriotic instruction is a form of compelled belief.
e: Rule: Government may not compel anyone to affirm a belief; it may pursue unity by persuasion and example, not compulsion. Barnette overruled Minersville School District v. Gobitis (1940).
oe: Correct. Barnette is a speech case: no official may "prescribe what shall be orthodox" or force citizens to "confess by word or act their faith therein." The result didn't depend on the objectors' religion.
Barnette didn't create a religious exemption. It held that no one, religious or secular, can be compelled to affirm a belief.
The Court rejected rational-basis review. Speech and worship may be restricted only to prevent "grave and immediate danger."
Barnette expressly allowed teaching history and civics and acquainting students with the salute. Only compelled affirmation was barred.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment overview — Compelled belief · Barnette

q: In Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, what test did the Court use for the Establishment Clause, and how did it apply it to the coach's prayer?
o: Any religious expression by a public employee at a school event is coercive, but the coach's prayer was protected by the Free Speech Clause.
The endorsement test governs, and a reasonable observer would not see a coach's prayer as the school endorsing religion.
The Lemon test still governs, and the prayer failed its purpose prong, but the Free Exercise Clause took priority over the Establishment Clause.
History and tradition replaced Lemon and the endorsement test, and the brief, quiet, personal prayer, which no students joined, was not coercion.
e: Rule: Kennedy (2022): the Establishment Clause is interpreted by reference to history and tradition and bars coercion, which requires more than a public employee's visible religious exercise.
oe: The majority rejected the idea that visible religious conduct is coercive; treating it that way would be hostility to religion. The coach won on Free Exercise grounds.
The endorsement test was abandoned along with Lemon. The Court asked about coercion, judged by history and tradition.
The majority abandoned Lemon. And the Court said the two clauses are complementary; neither automatically trumps the other.
Correct. The Court abandoned Lemon and read the Establishment Clause by history and tradition. It bars coercion, and visible religious exercise by a teacher isn't coercion by itself.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment overview — Establishment Clause · coercion

q: Under Mahmoud v. Taylor, when does a public school policy trigger strict scrutiny even if it is neutral and generally applicable?
o: Whenever parents object on religious grounds to any book or lesson in school.
Only when the school offers no private-school or homeschooling alternative that the parents could reasonably use instead.
When it substantially interferes with a child's religious development, a fact-specific Yoder-type burden.
Only when the policy compels students to recite or affirm a belief, as the flag salute did in Barnette.
e: Rule: Mahmoud (2025): if a school policy substantially interferes with a child's religious development (a Yoder-type burden), strict scrutiny applies even to a neutral, generally applicable policy; the inquiry is fact-intensive.
oe: The majority stressed limits. The parents sought to opt out of a specific requirement, not to micromanage the curriculum, and the inquiry is fact-intensive. The dissent warned the rule lacked a limiting principle.
The Court rejected private school or homeschooling as an answer. It is costly, and parents already fund the public schools.
Correct. The Court treated the parents' religious upbringing of their children as protected religious exercise and found the same "objective danger" as in Wisconsin v. Yoder.
Mahmoud recast Barnette as an "especially egregious" example and held that protection isn't limited to compelled affirmation. That narrower view was the dissent's.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment overview — Parental rights · Mahmoud

q: Which factor did the Mahmoud majority treat as "highly relevant" in distinguishing the high school students in Kennedy v. Bremerton School District from the elementary students in Mahmoud v. Taylor?
o: Whether the government actor was a teacher or a coach, since coaches have less authority over students than classroom teachers.
Whether the objecting families belonged to a religion that the school district had previously accommodated with an opt-out.
Whether the challenged conduct occurred during instructional time or at an extracurricular event held after the school day.
The children's age, along with normative content taught by trusted teachers, as opposed to passive observation of a coach's private prayer.
e: Rule: On the coercion spectrum, Barnette (compelled affirmation) is the clearest case; Kennedy and Mahmoud fight over how far below that line coercion reaches, with age a key factor.
oe: The Court didn't distinguish coaches from teachers by authority. It focused on age, normative instruction, and government instruction versus permitted private expression.
Prior accommodation of a particular faith wasn't the distinction. The board's other opt-outs mattered to strict scrutiny, not to whether there was coercion.
Timing wasn't the distinction the majority drew. Its focus was the students' age and the normative content of instruction.
Correct. Footnote 8 called age "highly relevant." Young children taught unmistakably normative books by teachers differ from high schoolers watching a coach pray quietly.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment overview — Coercion synthesis · Kennedy vs. Mahmoud

q: Why does the casebook have students read Justice Brandeis's concurrence in Whitney v. California?
o: For its account of First Amendment values: the remedy for evil counsels is good ones, and fear breeds repression.
Because it states the current test for incitement, which requires intent, imminence, and likelihood.
Because it adopts the clear and present danger test, which still governs prosecutions for advocating violence.
Because Justice Brandeis dissented and argued that the Criminal Syndicalism Act was unconstitutional on its face.
e: Rule: Brandeis's Whitney concurrence: liberty is an end and a means; public discussion is a political duty; the remedy for harmful speech is more speech.
oe: Correct. The concurrence is read for values, not doctrine. Counterspeech, not coerced silence, is the remedy. The Whitney majority itself was overruled by Brandenburg v. Ohio.
That test comes from Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969), which overruled the Whitney majority. Brandeis's opinion is read for values.
Clear and present danger was the older test. Brandenburg replaced it in practice.
Brandeis concurred in the result; he didn't dissent. The casebook reads his passage for its values.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment overview — Values · Whitney (Brandeis, J., concurring)

q: A state university requires all graduates at its optional commencement ceremony to stand for the national anthem. A student wants to stay seated to protest military policy. Under the outline's analysis, which point most helps the student?
o: Because the graduates are adults, the university's interest in instilling patriotism is weaker than in an elementary school.
Because attendance is optional, the rule is a permissible time, place, and manner regulation.
Forcing a choice between a major life event and a compelled gesture still looks coercive under Mahmoud.
Because the objection is political rather than religious, the Free Exercise Clause requires the university to grant an exemption.
e: Rule: Barnette bars compelling a "confession by act"; Mahmoud rejected the argument that objectors can simply go elsewhere.
oe: Adult status actually cuts against the student. It's one way the case differs from Barnette's schoolchildren.
Optional attendance helps the university, not the student, and a rule compelling a gesture isn't a content-neutral TPM rule.
Correct. Mahmoud v. Taylor rejected "just go elsewhere" as an answer, and standing is a "confession by act" in a patriotic ritual. The outline calls the case close.
Political objections are protected by the Speech Clause, as in West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette, not by Free Exercise.
topic: Ch. 1 · First Amendment overview — Stretch · anthem at graduation

q: Under Employment Division v. Smith, when must the government grant a religious exemption from a law that burdens religious conduct?
o: Only when the law burdens a practice that was widely accepted at the founding, under a history-and-tradition test.
Generally never, if the law is neutral and generally applicable; the Free Exercise Clause bars targeting religion, not incidental burdens.
Whenever the burden on a sincere religious practice is substantial and the government can't satisfy strict scrutiny.
Whenever the religious practice is central to the faith, as the sacramental use of peyote was to the Native American Church.
e: Rule: Smith (1990): the Free Exercise Clause does not require exemptions from neutral, generally applicable laws that incidentally burden religion.
oe: Smith turned on neutrality and general applicability, not founding-era practice. History and tradition is the Kennedy v. Bremerton School District test for the Establishment Clause.

Correct. Religious belief is absolutely protected, but religious conduct is protected only from laws that target it because it is religious. A "private right to ignore generally applicable laws" would be a "constitutional anomaly."
That's the RFRA standard Congress enacted in response to Smith. It is statutory, not the constitutional rule.
Smith rejected any centrality inquiry, and Smith and Black lost despite the ritual's importance.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Free Exercise · Smith

q: In Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah, why were the animal-killing ordinances not neutral or generally applicable?
o: They regulated religious belief rather than religious conduct, which the Free Exercise Clause absolutely protects.
They were enacted without a public hearing, so the city couldn't show it had considered less restrictive alternatives.
Exemptions for fishing, hunting, and pest control left Santeria sacrifice as the real target.
They imposed criminal penalties, which always trigger strict scrutiny.
e: Rule: A law that burdens only religiously motivated conduct, shown by exemptions for comparable secular conduct, is not neutral or generally applicable and must survive strict scrutiny.
oe: The ordinances regulated conduct (killing animals). They failed because they burdened only religiously motivated conduct.
Procedure wasn't the problem. The text's exemptions showed the laws targeted religious conduct.
Correct. The ordinances were underinclusive for both interests the city claimed. Society imposed on Santeria worshippers what it wouldn't impose on itself.
Criminal penalties don't trigger strict scrutiny on their own. Smith involved a criminal drug law that survived because it was neutral.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Neutrality · Lukumi

q: What was the basis for the Court's ruling for the baker in Masterpiece Cakeshop v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission?
o: The antidiscrimination law was not generally applicable because it contained a system of discretionary exemptions.
The First Amendment gives businesses a general right to refuse services for weddings that conflict with the owner's faith.
A wedding cake is the baker's own speech, so requiring him to make it was compelled speech that failed strict scrutiny.
The Commission applied a neutral law with hostility, disparaging religion and treating comparable bakers' objections more favorably.
e: Rule: Masterpiece (2018): official hostility to religion, or treating a religious objection worse than comparable objections, violates the Free Exercise Clause.
oe: Discretionary exemptions were the problem in Fulton v. City of Philadelphia. Masterpiece turned on hostility in applying the law.
The ruling was narrow. The Court didn't resolve the tension with antidiscrimination law and said states can generally protect equal access to goods and services.
The Court decided the case on Free Exercise grounds (hostility). It didn't rest on compelled speech.

Correct. Even a neutral law must be applied neutrally. Commissioners called religious justification "despicable" rhetoric, and three bakers who refused anti-same-sex-marriage messages were found to have acted lawfully.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Neutrality · Masterpiece

q: Philadelphia's foster-care contract let the Commissioner grant exceptions to its nondiscrimination requirement in her "sole discretion," but none had ever been granted. Under Fulton v. City of Philadelphia, what follows?
o: The policy is generally applicable, because a discretionary exception that has never been used has no effect on anyone.
The policy isn't generally applicable, because a system of discretionary exemptions counts even if unused.
The Court overruled Employment Division v. Smith and applied strict scrutiny to every burden on religious exercise.
The policy is generally applicable, but the city loses because it acted with open hostility toward Catholic doctrine.
e: Rule: Fulton (2021): discretionary, individualized exemptions make a policy not generally applicable; strict scrutiny asks about denying this particular claimant an exemption.
oe: Fulton held the opposite: the existence of the discretionary system defeats general applicability.
Correct. The power to grant exceptions counts even if unused. Strict scrutiny then asks whether the city has a compelling interest in denying this claimant an exemption.
The Court expressly declined to overrule Smith. It found the policy not generally applicable under Smith's own framework.
Hostility was Masterpiece Cakeshop's rationale. Fulton turned on the discretionary exemption system.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — General applicability · Fulton

q: Under Tandon v. Newsom, how does a court decide whether a regulation treats religious exercise worse than "comparable" secular activity?
o: Comparability is judged by risk to the government's interest; favoring any comparable secular activity triggers strict scrutiny.
A regulation triggers strict scrutiny only if it treats religious exercise worse than most secular activities.
Compare only activities in the same setting, so at-home worship is compared only with at-home secular gatherings.
Courts defer to the state's public-health judgment unless the regulation was motivated by animus toward religion.
e: Rule: Tandon (2021): a regulation triggers strict scrutiny whenever it treats any comparable secular activity, judged by risk, more favorably than religious exercise.
oe: Correct. It doesn't matter that some secular activities are treated as badly. The state must show the religious activity is riskier even with the same precautions.
One comparable secular activity treated better is enough. It doesn't matter that some secular activities are treated equally badly.
That was the dissent's view ("apples and watermelons"). The per curiam compared activities by risk, not setting.
Tandon required the state to justify the difference, and it said the state can't assume the worst about worship while assuming the best about work.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Comparability · Tandon

q: Maine paid tuition at private schools for families without a public high school, but only at "nonsectarian" schools. Under Carson v. Makin, which statement is correct?
o: Once Maine chose to subsidize private schooling, it couldn't exclude schools because they are religious, even if the funds pay for religious instruction.
Including religious schools would violate the Establishment Clause, so Maine was required to exclude them.
Maine could exclude religious schools that use funds for religious instruction, though not schools that are merely religiously affiliated.
Maine had to create a public religious school option so that families who wanted religious education would be treated equally.
e: Rule: Carson (2022), completing the Trinity Lutheran and Espinoza trilogy: if a state subsidizes private entities, it may not exclude religious ones because they're religious; it may end the program instead.
oe: Correct. Excluding religious entities from a generally available benefit penalizes free exercise. An interest in separating church and state more strictly than the federal Constitution requires isn't compelling.
Under Zelman v. Simmons-Harris, aid reaching religious schools through parents' genuine, independent choice doesn't violate the Establishment Clause.
Carson rejected the status-versus-use distinction. The exclusion was invalid even though the funds would pay for religious instruction.
Maine isn't required to fund private education at all. States may keep public schools strictly secular.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Funding · Carson

q: The outline identifies two "wrinkles" in Free Exercise doctrine. Which pair is correct?
o: Strict scrutiny for laws burdening religious belief, and rational basis for laws burdening religious conduct of any kind.
Hybrid rights always get strict scrutiny, and religious speech beats secular speech.
Exemptions for religious employers from all employment laws, and exemptions for clergy from compelled testimony.
Parental religious upbringing (Yoder; Mahmoud), and disfavoring religion only to avoid an Establishment violation.
e: Rule: Wrinkle 1: parental religious education (Yoder; Mahmoud). Wrinkle 2: Establishment Clause avoidance justifies disfavoring religion only when necessary (Carson).
oe: Belief is absolutely protected; conduct is protected from targeting (Smith). Neither describes the two wrinkles.
Smith mentioned hybrid rights to explain past cases, but neither statement is one of the two wrinkles. Barnette protects secular speech equally.
Neither is one of the outline's two wrinkles in Free Exercise doctrine.

Correct. Wrinkle 1 applies strict scrutiny even to generally applicable laws. Wrinkle 2 lets government disfavor religion only when the Establishment Clause requires it, not to separate church and state more strictly (Carson v. Makin).
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Two wrinkles

q: Which sequence correctly describes the evolution of the Establishment Clause funding cases?
o: The Lemon era required inclusion; Zelman permitted exclusion; the modern trilogy restored the Lemon rule.
Zelman required states to include religious schools; Carson v. Makin then permitted states to exclude them if they had a compelling interest.
Exclusion permitted (Lemon era), inclusion permitted (Zelman), then inclusion required (the Carson trilogy).
Public funds may never reach religious schools, directly or through parents.
e: Rule: Funding stages: exclusion permitted (Lemon era) → inclusion permitted (Zelman, 2002) → inclusion required (Trinity Lutheran 2017, Espinoza 2020, Carson 2022).
oe: Under Lemon, states could exclude religious entities to avoid the appearance of support. The trilogy moved away from that.
The order is reversed. Zelman permitted inclusion; Carson required it.
Correct. The Court went from permitting exclusion, to permitting inclusion, to requiring inclusion once a state subsidizes private entities.
Zelman v. Simmons-Harris upheld vouchers reaching parochial schools through parents' genuine, independent choice.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Establishment Clause · funding stages

q: Which statement about the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA) is correct?
o: It binds state and local governments but not the federal government.
It requires strict scrutiny for substantial burdens on religion, but now binds only the federal government.
It overruled Employment Division v. Smith, so the Free Exercise Clause now requires strict scrutiny for all burdens on religion.
It was struck down entirely in City of Boerne v. Flores, so religious claimants must rely on Smith alone.
e: Rule: RFRA (1993): strict scrutiny for substantial burdens on religion, as a statute; it binds the federal government only (City of Boerne v. Flores, 1997).
oe: Boerne held the opposite: RFRA can't bind states and localities but still binds the federal government.
Correct. RFRA was Congress's response to Smith. Boerne held it exceeded Congress's power as to state and local governments. RLUIPA, a narrower statute, binds the states.
A statute can't overrule a constitutional decision. RFRA creates statutory protection; Smith remains the constitutional rule.
Boerne invalidated RFRA only as applied to states and localities. It still applies federally (e.g., Burwell v. Hobby Lobby).
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — RFRA and Boerne

q: The "play in the joints" between the Religion Clauses had two concepts. What is their status today?
o: Both were abandoned when Kennedy v. Bremerton School District overruled Lemon.
Declining to fund religion survives, but accommodation beyond Free Exercise was rejected in Cutter v. Wilkinson.
Both concepts remain fully alive, so states may freely exclude religious schools from tuition programs.
Accommodation beyond Free Exercise survives; declining to fund religion is in retreat.
e: Rule: Play in the joints: accommodation beyond Free Exercise is alive (Cutter, 2005); declining to fund religion to avoid Establishment concerns is in retreat (Carson, 2022).
oe: Kennedy abandoned Lemon, but accommodation beyond Free Exercise (concept #1) remains alive.
The status is reversed. Cutter unanimously upheld RLUIPA's accommodations.
Carson v. Makin held that a state may not exclude religious schools from a generally available tuition benefit.
Correct. Concept #1 survives in RFRA, RLUIPA, and Cutter v. Wilkinson. Concept #2 was rejected in the Trinity Lutheran, Espinoza, and Carson trilogy.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Play in the joints

q: In Wooley v. Maynard, why couldn't New Hampshire require drivers to display "Live Free or Die" on their license plates?
o: The motto was religious in character, and the Establishment Clause bars the state from endorsing religious messages.
The state may not make a person carry its ideological message on private property for others to see.
License plates are a public forum, and one slogan is viewpoint discrimination.
Displaying a motto is the same as saluting a flag, so the case was squarely controlled by Barnette with no further analysis needed.
e: Rule: Wooley (1977): the state may not compel a person to be the courier of its ideological message on private property; footnote 15 distinguishes "In God We Trust" on currency.
oe: The motto isn't religious, and the Court used a speech rationale that protects any objector, though the Maynards were Jehovah's Witnesses.
Correct. The car becomes a "mobile billboard." The interests failed: identification can use plate numbers, and promoting state pride is an ideological interest.
Wooley is a compelled speech case, not a forum case. Whether plates are government speech came up later, in Walker v. Texas Division.
The Court said passive display is less than a salute but the difference is "one of degree." It still analyzed the state's interests.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause overview — Compelled speech · Wooley

q: Skokie, home to thousands of Holocaust survivors, passed ordinances to block a planned Nazi march. In Collin v. Smith, why did the Seventh Circuit strike them down?
o: The ordinances were content based, and listeners' psychic trauma can't justify banning a peaceful march.
The ordinances were content neutral but failed intermediate scrutiny because they left no alternative channels for the march.
Nazi symbols were fighting words, but the village failed to show the march would occur near an audience likely to fight.
The ordinances were valid but applied selectively to the marchers.
e: Rule: Government may not ban a peaceful demonstration because of its message; listener protection is allowed only for intrusions into the home or a truly captive audience.
oe: Correct. Residents weren't a captive audience; they could avoid Village Hall for half an hour. Shock that flows from the ideas themselves is not a basis for suppression.
The court found the ordinances content-based: the village objected to who was marching and what they said.
The village conceded it expected no violence, so the case fell outside both Brandenburg and Chaplinsky. The court didn't treat the symbols as fighting words.
The court held the ordinances themselves unconstitutional, not merely their application.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause overview — Content-based restrictions · Collin

q: Indianapolis banned sexually explicit material depicting women as subordinate, but allowed explicit material depicting women as equals. What did American Booksellers Ass'n v. Hudnut hold?
o: The ordinance was invalid only because it was vague about which materials depict women as subordinate.
The ordinance was valid because the material it covered was obscene under the three-part Miller test.
The ordinance was unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination, even accepting that such depictions perpetuate women's subordination.
The ordinance was valid because preventing harm to women is a compelling interest and the law was narrowly tailored.
e: Rule: Government may not favor one viewpoint and silence the other, even when the disfavored speech causes real social harm.
oe: The court rested on viewpoint discrimination, not vagueness.
The ordinance didn't track Miller. It had no prurient-interest, offensiveness, or work-as-a-whole requirement, and value was irrelevant.
Correct. Judge Easterbrook accepted the harm but said it only shows the power of speech. Otherwise government becomes "the great censor and director of which thoughts are good for us."
The court never reached tailoring. Viewpoint discrimination is fatal even when the government is right about the harm.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause overview — Viewpoint discrimination · Hudnut

q: In United States v. Stevens, the government argued that depictions of animal cruelty should be unprotected because their value is outweighed by their social costs. How did the Court respond?
o: The balancing test is correct, but the government failed to prove that crush videos cause measurable harm to animals.
New categories may be recognized, but only by Congress through specific findings, not by courts.
Animal cruelty depictions are unprotected, but the statute was struck because it lacked an exception for works of serious value.
It called that test "startling and dangerous"; unprotected categories must be historically recognized.
e: Rule: Stevens (2010): content-based restrictions are presumptively invalid unless the speech falls within a historically recognized unprotected category; courts don't create new categories by balancing.
oe: The Court rejected balancing as the method for recognizing categories. It wasn't an evidentiary failure.
The Court held that neither courts nor legislatures may add categories by balancing value against costs.
The Court refused to recognize the category at all, and the statute did contain an exceptions clause (it just didn't cover hunting videos).
Correct. The First Amendment already reflects the people's cost-benefit judgment, and there is no tradition of banning depictions of animal cruelty.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause overview — Unprotected categories · Stevens

q: Which statement best describes United States v. Alvarez (the Stolen Valor Act case)?
o: False statements of fact are unprotected, but the Act failed because it covered lies told in private as well as in public.
A majority applied intermediate scrutiny and found the Act too broad.
There's no general exception for false statements, and the usual remedy for a lie is the truth.
The Act was valid because lying about military honors is fraud, which has always been an unprotected category.
e: Rule: Alvarez (2012): no general exception for false statements; a content-based ban on lies must be "actually necessary," and counterspeech is the ordinary remedy.
oe: The plurality rejected a general exception for falsehoods. The Act's breadth (lies "whispered at home") was one reason it failed strict scrutiny.
There was no majority opinion. The plurality applied strict scrutiny; Breyer and Kagan concurred in the judgment under intermediate scrutiny.
Correct. Prior cases saying falsehood has no value involved cognizable harm (defamation, fraud). The Act targeted "falsity and nothing more," and counterspeech exposed Alvarez.
Alvarez sought no money or job. His lie was "a pathetic attempt to gain respect," not fraud.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause overview — False statements · Alvarez

q: When is a statute facially invalid under the First Amendment overbreadth doctrine, according to United States v. Hansen?
o: When the challenger shows the statute has no valid applications at all.
When it reaches a substantial amount of protected speech relative to its legitimate sweep.
When the challenger's own speech is protected and the statute fails to give fair notice of what it prohibits.
When any realistic application of the statute would reach protected speech, regardless of how many lawful applications it has.
e: Rule: Hansen (2023): a law is facially overbroad only if it prohibits a substantial amount of protected speech relative to its legitimate sweep; courts first adopt any fairly possible constitutional construction.
oe: That's the ordinary facial-challenge standard (Salerno). Overbreadth is a special, more lenient doctrine for speech.
Correct. Overbreadth is "strong medicine." The unconstitutional applications must be realistic and the ratio lopsided, and courts first construe the statute (constitutional avoidance).
That mixes up vagueness with overbreadth. Overbreadth lets a litigant whose own speech is unprotected assert others' rights.
One or a few protected applications aren't enough. The ratio of unconstitutional to legitimate applications must be lopsided.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause overview — Overbreadth · Hansen

q: Why was the animal-cruelty statute in United States v. Stevens facially invalid while the "encourage or induce" statute in United States v. Hansen was upheld?
o: Stevens's statute realistically reached hunting videos; Hansen's covered only solicitation and facilitation.
Hansen's own speech was fraud, so he couldn't raise overbreadth at all.
Stevens involved a criminal statute while Hansen involved a civil one, and criminal statutes get stricter overbreadth review.
The government promised to prosecute only extreme cases in Hansen but made no similar promise in Stevens.
e: Rule: Overbreadth turns on construction and the ratio of realistic protected applications to the statute's legitimate sweep.
oe: Correct. Construction drove the results. In Stevens the protected applications were realistic and numerous; in Hansen the remaining concerns were fanciful.
Overbreadth lets a litigant whose own speech is unprotected raise others' rights. Hansen could raise it; he just lost.
Both were federal criminal statutes. The difference was statutory construction and the resulting ratio.
In Stevens the Court rejected reliance on such a promise: the First Amendment doesn't leave us "at the mercy of noblesse oblige."
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause overview — Overbreadth · Stevens vs. Hansen

q: Which list contains only categories of speech the Court treats as historically unprotected?
o: Fighting words, profanity, indecent broadcasts, violent video games, and child pornography.
Incitement, hate speech, obscenity, false statements of fact, and depictions of animal cruelty.
Incitement, fighting words, true threats, child pornography, obscenity, and fraud.
Obscenity, commercial advertising, flag burning, true threats, and speech integral to crime.
e: Rule: Historically unprotected: incitement, fighting words, grave threats government may prevent, true threats, speech integral to crime, child pornography, obscenity, defamation (within limits), and fraud.
oe: Profanity is protected (Cohen v. California), Pacifica is a narrow broadcast exception rather than a category, and Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association refused to make violence a category.
Hate speech is generally protected (R.A.V.; Collin), false statements as such are protected (Alvarez), and the Court refused to add animal cruelty (Stevens).
Correct. These appear in the outline's table of historically unprotected categories.
Commercial speech is protected (Virginia Pharmacy Board) and flag burning is protected expressive conduct (Texas v. Johnson).
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause overview — Historically unprotected categories

q: Under the outline's speech checklist, what must the government show when a content-based restriction doesn't fall within an unprotected category?
o: That the speech is false or harmful, since false and harmful speech is categorically unprotected.
A compelling interest and a restriction that is actually necessary and least restrictive.
A legitimate interest and a rational relationship between the restriction and that interest.
An important interest and that the restriction doesn't burden substantially more speech than necessary.
e: Rule: Content-based restrictions on protected speech get strict scrutiny: a compelling interest, actual necessity, and least restrictive means.
oe: The outline stresses that false, heinous, and harmful speech is often protected, because of distrust of government line-drawing.
Correct. Content-based restrictions are presumptively invalid and get strict scrutiny; the government usually loses.
Rational basis applies to unprotected speech, not to content-based restrictions on protected speech.
That's intermediate scrutiny, used for content-neutral rules (Ch. 9) and for some incidental burdens.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause overview — Speech framework · strict scrutiny

q: A state rejects a vanity license plate reading "FCANCER" while allowing other vanity plates. How does the outline classify that rejection?
o: Viewpoint-based, the worst form of content discrimination, subject to strict scrutiny; a cancer survivor won in 2024.
Permissible indecency regulation under FCC v. Pacifica Foundation, because license plates are seen by children.
Content neutral, because the state applies the same profanity rule to every plate regardless of topic.
Unprotected obscenity, because the plate's message is patently offensive under contemporary community standards.
e: Rule: Viewpoint-based restrictions are the worst form of content discrimination and get strict scrutiny.
oe: Correct. The outline's chart lists the FCANCER plate as viewpoint-based. Calling speech "profane" generally doesn't justify restricting it.
Pacifica is a narrow broadcast exception. It doesn't make profanity on plates regulable.
Rejecting a plate because of its message about cancer turns on content and viewpoint, not on a neutral time, place, or manner.
Profanity isn't obscenity. Miller requires prurient appeal and depiction of sexual conduct.
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement, fighting words & prior restraints — Scrutiny by type of rule

q: Under Brandenburg v. Ohio, advocacy of force or lawbreaking may be punished only if what is shown?
o: It advocates the moral propriety or necessity of violence as a means of political change.
It has a tendency to produce violence at some point in the future, judged by a reasonable listener.
It creates a clear and present danger of a substantive evil that the legislature has a right to prevent.
It is directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action and is likely to produce such action.
e: Rule: Brandenburg (1969): advocacy may be punished only if directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action and likely to produce it; it overruled Whitney.
oe: Abstract teaching of the moral propriety or even necessity of force is protected; preparing a group for violent action is not.
Bad tendency was the Whitney-era approach. Brandenburg requires imminence and likelihood, plus intent.
That older test was used to affirm WWI dissidents' convictions. Brandenburg replaced it in practice.
Correct. Intent, imminence, and likelihood are all required. Ohio's law punished mere advocacy with none of those elements.
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement, fighting words & prior restraints — Incitement · Brandenburg

q: In Terminiello v. City of Chicago, why was the speaker's breach-of-the-peace conviction reversed?
o: The jury instruction let it convict merely for speech that stirred anger or invited dispute.
The crowd outside was hostile, and the heckler's veto doctrine bars punishing a speaker for an audience's reaction.
The speech was a sermon, protected by the Free Exercise Clause.
The ordinance was a prior restraint because it required speakers to obtain a permit before addressing a crowd.
e: Rule: Terminiello (1949): speech may not be punished merely for stirring anger, inviting dispute, or creating unrest.
oe: Correct. Speech may best serve its purpose when it stirs people to anger. Punishment requires a clear and present danger of a serious evil far above inconvenience.
The heckler's veto cases are Cox v. Louisiana and Edwards v. South Carolina. Terminiello turned on the instruction.
Terminiello was a free speech case about the breadth of the jury instruction, not a Free Exercise case.
No permit or prior restraint was at issue. The defect was the instruction's definition of breach of the peace.
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement, fighting words & prior restraints — Breach of peace · Terminiello

q: Peaceful civil rights protesters are arrested because a hostile crowd nearby might turn violent, though police on the scene could control the crowd. What does the outline say?
o: The arrests are valid under Chaplinsky, because the protest provoked the crowd.
The arrests are valid because protests near government buildings are a nonpublic forum where speech may be restricted.
The arrests are valid if officers reasonably believed violence was imminent, under the Brandenburg incitement test.
The convictions fall, because there's no heckler's veto when the police can control the crowd.
e: Rule: No heckler's veto: government may not silence peaceful speakers because a hostile audience might react violently when police can control it.
oe: Fighting words are personal insults likely to provoke the listener to attack the speaker immediately. Peaceful protest isn't that.
A peaceful demonstration near government is speech "in its classic form."
Brandenburg concerns the speaker's intent to incite lawless action. Here the threat came from the audience.
Correct. In Cox, 75 to 80 armed police separated the protesters from a hostile crowd. In Edwards, police protection "was at all times sufficient."
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement, fighting words & prior restraints — Fighting words and hostile audiences

q: St. Paul banned symbols arousing anger "on the basis of race, color, creed, religion or gender," construed to reach only fighting words. Why did R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul strike it down?
o: Cross burning is protected expression that can never be punished.
St. Paul singled out a subset of fighting words based on their topic, which is content discrimination.
Fighting words are no longer unprotected, so any ban on them must survive strict scrutiny.
The ordinance was not limited to fighting words, so it reached a substantial amount of protected hate speech.
e: Rule: R.A.V. (1992): government may ban an entire unprotected category but may not single out a subset based on topic or viewpoint.
oe: R.A.V. didn't hold that. It struck the ordinance for selecting a subset of an unprotected category by topic.

Correct. Government may ban all fighting words for what makes them proscribable, but not just those on disfavored topics. The ordinance didn't reach fighting words based on political affiliation or sexual orientation.
The fighting-words category survives, though no restriction has been upheld on that theory since 1942.
The Court accepted the state court's construction limiting it to fighting words. The problem was content discrimination within that category.
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement, fighting words & prior restraints — Fighting words · R.A.V.

q: Which statement about prior restraints is correct under Near v. Minnesota and the Pentagon Papers case?
o: Prior restraints are subject to the same standard as subsequent punishment, so a newspaper may be enjoined from publishing anything it could be punished for.
Near held that newspapers criticizing public officials may be enjoined if the criticism is false and malicious.
A prior restraint carries a heavy presumption of invalidity; Near's wartime dictum (troop locations, sailing dates) is the only exception and has never been applied.
Prior restraints are valid whenever the executive branch certifies that publication would harm national security.
e: Rule: Prior restraints are presumptively unconstitutional (Near, 1931; New York Times Co. v. United States, 1971); the government bears a heavy burden.
oe: The Framers especially opposed prior restraints. They carry a heavier presumption than after-the-fact punishment.
Near struck the injunction against The Saturday Press, which criticized law enforcement as corrupt.
Correct. In New York Times Co. v. United States, a general claim of harm to national security didn't carry the government's heavy burden.
The Pentagon Papers Court refused to accept a general national-security claim.
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement, fighting words & prior restraints — Prior restraints · Near

q: Which reason does the outline give, through Thomas Emerson's work quoted by the ACLU, for why prior restraints are worse than punishment after publication?
o: They are always content based, while punishments after publication are always content neutral.
They stop speech before it happens and are imposed "by a stroke of the pen," without trial safeguards.
They require the government to prove actual malice, which is harder to show before publication.
They apply only to the press, so they discriminate among speakers based on their identity.
e: Rule: Prior restraints are especially disfavored because they stop speech in advance, sweep broadly, lack procedural safeguards, and invite excess.
oe: Both prior restraints and subsequent punishments can be content based. That isn't the distinction.
Correct. Emerson also noted that prior restraints allow less public criticism and drive toward excess.
Actual malice is the defamation standard from New York Times v. Sullivan. It isn't why prior restraints are disfavored.
Prior restraints aren't limited to the press, and speaker discrimination wasn't Emerson's point.
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement, fighting words & prior restraints — Pentagon Papers · why prior restraints are worse

q: In every Chapter 4 case, the argument that the speech was unprotected failed. Which pairing of case and reason is correct?
o: Cohen v. California: the jacket wasn't a direct personal insult likely to provoke violence.
Collin v. Smith: the march was a religious procession protected by Free Exercise.
R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul: the cross burning was protected because it was not directed at any particular person.
Brandenburg v. Ohio: the speech was protected because it occurred on private farmland rather than in a public forum.
e: Rule: Know why each unprotected-category argument failed: Terminiello (no imminence), Brandenburg (mere advocacy), Cohen (no personal insult), Cox and Edwards (police could control the crowd), Collin (no expected violence), R.A.V. (topic-based subset), Near and the Pentagon Papers (heavy presumption).
oe: Correct. "Fuck the Draft" was a political message, not an insult directed at anyone present.
In Collin, the village conceded it expected no violence, taking the case outside both incitement and fighting words.
R.A.V. failed because the ordinance banned only a topic-based subset of fighting words.
Brandenburg failed because Ohio's law punished mere advocacy with no intent, imminence, or likelihood requirement.
topic: Ch. 4 · Incitement, fighting words & prior restraints — Synthesis · why unprotected-category arguments failed

q: Under Counterman v. Colorado, what mental state must the prosecution prove in a true-threats case?
o: Purpose: the speaker must have intended the recipient to feel threatened.
Knowledge: the speaker must have known with certainty that the recipient would view the message as a threat.
None: a statement is a true threat if a reasonable person would see it as threatening, regardless of the speaker's mind.
At least recklessness about whether the words would be understood as a threat of violence.
e: Rule: Counterman (2023): true threats are unprotected, but the speaker must have been at least reckless as to whether the words would be viewed as threatening.
oe: That was the Sotomayor concurrence's position (joined in part by Gorsuch). The majority chose recklessness.
The Court didn't require knowledge. Recklessness, consciously accepting a substantial risk, suffices.
That purely objective test was the dissent's view (Barrett, Thomas). The majority vacated Counterman's conviction under it.
Correct. A true threat is judged by how a reasonable recipient would understand it, but the First Amendment also requires a subjective element. Recklessness balances chilling against harm to victims.
topic: Ch. 5 · True threats & speech integral to crime — True threats · Counterman

q: The outline describes "mens rea as speech protection." Which pairing of doctrine and required mental state is correct?
o: Brandenburg requires recklessness; Counterman requires intent; Williams requires only negligence.
Mens rea requirements apply only to civil defamation cases, not to criminal prosecutions for speech.
Brandenburg: intent. Counterman: recklessness. United States v. Williams: belief and intent.
All unprotected categories use a purely objective, reasonable-person test with no mental-state element.
e: Rule: Mens rea as speech protection: Brandenburg (intent), Counterman (recklessness), Williams (belief and intent), and, for defamation, actual malice.
oe: The pairings are scrambled. Brandenburg requires intent, Counterman recklessness, and Williams belief and intent.
Brandenburg, Counterman, and Williams were all criminal cases with mens rea requirements.
Correct. Culpable mental states give honest speakers "breathing room," at the cost of letting some unprotected speech go unpunished.
The Court often forbids penalizing speech without a culpable mental state. That's the outline's point.
topic: Ch. 5 · True threats & speech integral to crime — Mens rea as speech protection

q: Under United States v. Williams, which statement would a federal pandering statute reach?
o: A news report describing how child pornography rings distribute material online.
An offer to sell a specific file that the seller describes as, and believes to be, child pornography.
A blog post arguing that possession of child pornography should be legalized.
A general statement that "I encourage people to obtain such material," with no particular item identified.
e: Rule: Williams (2008): offers to provide or requests to obtain contraband are categorically unprotected; abstract advocacy is not.
oe: Reporting isn't an offer or request for contraband. It's protected speech.
Correct. Offers and requests for contraband are speech integral to crime, unprotected under Giboney. They're punishable even if the belief turns out to be mistaken.
Abstract advocacy of illegality stays protected (Brandenburg). "Promotes" means recommending a particular item with intent to initiate a transfer.
The Court said "promotes" doesn't reach even "I encourage you to obtain it." It requires a specific item and intent to transfer.
topic: Ch. 5 · True threats & speech integral to crime — Speech integral to crime · Williams

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes vagueness from overbreadth?
o: Overbreadth lets a litigant challenge only applications to his own speech, while vagueness protects third parties.
Vagueness comes from the First Amendment and overbreadth from Due Process; both require that the law have no valid applications.
A law is void for vagueness whenever close cases exist about whether particular conduct is covered.
Vagueness, from Due Process, asks whether a law is unclear; overbreadth, from the First Amendment, asks whether it reaches too much protected speech.
e: Rule: Vagueness (Due Process): no fair notice or standardless enforcement. Overbreadth (First Amendment): a substantial amount of protected speech relative to the law's legitimate sweep.
oe: Overbreadth is the doctrine that lets a litigant assert third parties' rights (Stevens; Hansen).
The sources are reversed, and neither requires that a law have no valid applications.
Williams said close cases don't make a law vague. Perfect clarity has never been required; the question is indeterminacy about what fact must be proved.
Correct. Both aim to prevent chilling. In First Amendment cases the Court relaxes the rule that someone clearly covered can't complain of vagueness as to others.
topic: Ch. 5 · True threats & speech integral to crime — Vagueness vs. overbreadth

q: Why did the Fourth Circuit allow an aiding-and-abetting suit against the publisher of Hit Man in Rice v. Paladin Enterprises?
o: Publishers have reduced First Amendment protection compared with news organizations, which are always protected.
The book was obscene, so the publisher's intent didn't matter.
Paladin stipulated that it intended to assist murderers, and the book was used as intended.
Any publisher of detailed instructions for committing a crime is liable when a reader uses them to commit it.
e: Rule: Speech, even publishing, that aids and abets a crime is unprotected where the publisher intended to assist criminals and the material was used exactly as intended.
oe: The court said news reporting is never a basis for liability, but publishers aren't specially disfavored. Intent was the key.
Obscenity wasn't at issue. The theory was aiding and abetting, a form of speech integral to crime.
Correct. The stipulations made the case unique. The court said evidence of intent will almost never exist without such stipulations, and copycat cases involving novels or films differ.
The court stressed that not all manuals qualify. Intent, detail, exhortation, and lack of legitimate purpose were all present.
topic: Ch. 5 · True threats & speech integral to crime — Aiding and abetting · Rice v. Paladin

q: In Garcia v. Character Technologies, why did the court decline to dismiss the wrongful-death suit on First Amendment grounds at the preliminary stage?
o: It wasn't prepared to hold that the chatbot's output reflected an expressive choice, so it might not be speech.
It held that AI companies have no First Amendment rights because they are not natural persons.
It held that users have no right to receive speech from a chatbot, so the companies couldn't assert their users' rights.
It held that the chatbot's messages were true threats and therefore unprotected.
e: Rule: Garcia (M.D. Fla. 2025): output counts as speech only if expressive; the court wasn't prepared to hold chatbot output is speech.
oe: Correct. Drawing on Justice Barrett's concurrence in Moody v. NetChoice, the court said output counts as speech only if it is expressive.
The court didn't deny corporations' speech rights. Its doubt was whether the output reflected human expressive choices.
The court said a distributor may assert its users' right to receive speech. The problem was whether the output was speech.
The court didn't classify the output as threats. The issue was whether the output was speech at all.
topic: Ch. 5 · True threats & speech integral to crime — AI output as speech · Garcia

q: Which statement is protected speech rather than speech integral to criminal conduct?
o: "Wait in the car; I'll signal you when the guard leaves so you can break in."
"Hand over your wallet or I'll hurt you."
"I'll sell you heroin for $100 tonight behind the gas station."
"Cocaine should be legal, and the drug war has failed."
e: Rule: Unprotected: speech that is the crime, offers or solicits illegal acts, or helps commit or conceal one. Abstract advocacy of illegality stays protected.
oe: Speech that helps commit a crime (aiding and abetting, conspiracy) is integral to criminal conduct.
The speech is the crime itself (robbery or extortion).
An offer to sell contraband is speech integral to crime, unprotected (Giboney; Williams).
Correct. Abstract advocacy of illegality is protected. Speech integral to crime is speech that is the crime, offers or solicits it, or helps commit or conceal it.
topic: Ch. 5 · True threats & speech integral to crime — Speech integral to crime · examples

q: Congress banned mailing unsolicited contraceptive ads to homes, citing the interest in helping parents control what their children see. What did Bolger v. Youngs Drug Products Corp. hold?
o: The ban is valid, because commercial speech gets no protection.
The ban fails only because the parental interest is insubstantial and not worth protecting.
The ban fails, because the government may not limit adults to reading only what is fit for children.
The ban is valid because mail enters the home, where privacy interests are strongest, as in FCC v. Pacifica Foundation.
e: Rule: Government can't shield adults from immoral content (except obscenity); it can protect kids only if adults keep access.
oe: Commercial speech is protected (Virginia Pharmacy Board), and the Court struck the ban.
The Court called helping parents "undoubtedly substantial." The ban failed because it swept in material suitable for adults.
Correct. Shielding adults from offense "carries little weight," and the trip "from mail box to trash can is an acceptable burden."
Pacifica was distinguished as narrow. Broadcasting is "uniquely pervasive" and accessible to children in a way mail isn't.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral speech — Who is protected · Bolger

q: What principle about unwilling viewers comes from Cohen v. California?
o: Unwilling viewers outside the home generally must avert their eyes rather than silence the speaker.
Offensive speech may be banned wherever women and children are present, because they are a captive audience.
Unwilling viewers may obtain an injunction against offensive speech if they show emotional distress.
Profanity is protected only when it is part of political speech; otherwise it is an unprotected category.
e: Rule: Profanity is protected; offended viewers outside the home generally must avert their eyes.
oe: Correct. Cohen's "Fuck the Draft" jacket in a courthouse corridor was protected; the outline's takeaway is that profanity is protected speech.
The Court reversed Cohen's conviction even though women and children were present.
Cohen offers no such remedy. The burden is on offended viewers to look away.
Profanity isn't an unprotected category. Calling speech profane or indecent generally doesn't make it restrictable.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral speech — Profanity · Cohen

q: What made FCC v. Pacifica Foundation an exception to the rule that indecent but non-obscene speech is protected?
o: The FCC imposed criminal penalties, and criminal penalties for profanity are always permitted on public airwaves.
Broadcasting is uniquely pervasive and accessible to children, a narrow nuisance rationale.
Radio stations are government speakers whose content the FCC controls.
The Carlin monologue was obscene under the Miller test.
e: Rule: Pacifica (1978): government may regulate indecent but non-obscene broadcasts because broadcasting is uniquely accessible to children; the holding is narrow.
oe: The FCC issued a declaratory order without formal sanctions. Criminal prosecution was expressly not decided.
Correct. Time of day, content, and medium matter: a nuisance may be "a pig in the parlor instead of the barnyard."
Pacifica was a private broadcaster. The rationale was broadcasting's pervasiveness and accessibility to children.
The Court treated the broadcast as indecent but not obscene. That's why the case is an exception.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral speech — Indecent broadcasting · Pacifica

q: Under Miller v. California, which prong most protects valuable works that contain explicit scenes?
o: Whether the work, taken as a whole, lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.
Whether the average person, applying contemporary community standards, finds that the work appeals to the prurient interest.
Whether a judge, viewing the work, would "know it when I see it," as Justice Stewart wrote.
Whether the work depicts sexual conduct in a patently offensive way.
e: Rule: Miller (1973): obscene only if (a) prurient appeal under community standards, (b) patently offensive depiction of sexual conduct defined by state law, and (c) the work as a whole lacks serious value.
oe: Correct. The outline says prong (c) matters most because it protects works that have value as a whole, even if isolated scenes seem obscene.
That's prong (a). "Prurient" means a shameful or morbid interest. But prong (c) is what protects valuable works.
Stewart's line from Jacobellis predates Miller and is not the test. Miller replaced that era's uncertainty with three prongs.
That's prong (b). Prong (c), the value inquiry, protects valuable works.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral speech — Obscenity · Miller test

q: Why did Renton v. Playtime Theatres apply only intermediate scrutiny to a zoning law confining adult theaters?
o: Adult films are obscene, so any regulation of adult theaters gets only rational-basis review.
The theaters' owners were corporations, which receive less First Amendment protection than individuals.
Zoning laws are always content neutral because they regulate land use rather than speech.
The law targeted secondary effects such as crime and property values, not the films' message.
e: Rule: Renton (1986): zoning that confines adult businesses gets intermediate scrutiny because it targets secondary effects, not the message.
oe: Many adult films aren't obscene under Miller. Renton applied intermediate scrutiny, not rational basis.
Corporate status played no role. The rationale was the law's aim at secondary effects.
The Court acknowledged the law was partly content based. Its secondary-effects purpose justified intermediate scrutiny.
Correct. The secondary-effects doctrine is narrow; the Court has refused to extend it beyond adult entertainment establishments.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral speech — Secondary effects · Renton

q: Why is child pornography made with real children unprotected even when it isn't obscene, according to New York v. Ferber?
o: Viewing it causes viewers to commit crimes against children, so it's a form of incitement.
It always appeals to the prurient interest and so automatically satisfies the Miller test for obscenity.
Its distribution is intrinsically related to the sexual abuse of the children used to make it.
It has no expressive content, so it isn't speech at all.
e: Rule: Ferber (1982): child pornography made with real children is unprotected because its distribution is intrinsically related to the abuse; the casebook likens the rationale to secondary effects.
oe: Ferber didn't rest on incitement or effects on viewers. Its rationale was the abuse of real children in production.
Ferber's point is that the material is unprotected without meeting Miller. New York's law didn't require obscenity.
Correct. Two links: the material is a permanent record whose circulation worsens the harm, and the distribution network must be closed to control production.
The Court said its value is "exceedingly modest, if not de minimis," not zero. It is speech but unprotected.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral speech — Child pornography · Ferber

q: Congress banned sexually explicit images that "appear to" depict minors, including computer-generated images. What did Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition hold?
o: The ban is valid because virtual images whet the appetites of abusers and so cause the same harm as real images.
The ban violates the First Amendment because Ferber's rationale depends on protecting real children exploited in production.
The ban is valid as applied to images indistinguishable from real children, because they're obscene.
The ban is invalid only because it lacked an exception for works with serious artistic value.
e: Rule: Free Speech Coalition (2002): Ferber doesn't extend to sexually explicit images made without real children; but offers to sell material believed to involve real children may be punished (Williams).
oe: The Court rejected that indirect-harm theory as outside Ferber's production-based rationale.
Correct. The law also banned speech regardless of serious value, and "appear to be under 18" exceeded many states' ages for marriage and consent.
The Court didn't uphold it for realistic images. Obscenity is a separate category with its own test.
The lack of a value inquiry was one problem, but the core holding was that Ferber doesn't reach images made without real children.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral speech — Virtual images · Free Speech Coalition

q: Why did Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton uphold Texas's age-verification law when Ashcroft v. ACLU had blocked COPA?
o: Paxton applied rational-basis review because sexually explicit material is unprotected for adults and children alike.
Paxton applied strict scrutiny but found the government had proved that filters don't work.
Paxton used intermediate scrutiny, since the burden on adults was only incidental.
Ashcroft II involved a ban on obscenity, while Paxton involved material that is merely indecent.
e: Rule: Paxton (2025): age verification for speech obscene as to minors gets intermediate scrutiny because its burden on adults is incidental; Texas's law satisfies it.
oe: The Court rejected rational basis: adults have a real, if incidentally burdened, right. It applied intermediate scrutiny.
Paxton didn't apply strict scrutiny. Under intermediate scrutiny, less restrictive alternatives don't defeat a legitimate legislative choice.
Correct. Ashcroft II applied strict scrutiny, under which effective, less restrictive filters doomed COPA. The outline asks whether Paxton effectively overruled Ashcroft II.
Both concerned material harmful or obscene as to minors. The difference was the standard of review.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral speech — Age-gating · Ashcroft II vs. Paxton

q: California banned selling violent video games to minors. Why did Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association strike it down?
o: There's no unprotected category for violence, and the law failed strict scrutiny.
Video games aren't speech, and the law failed rational-basis review.
The law was valid under Ginsberg v. New York, which lets states adjust unprotected categories for minors.
Minors have no First Amendment rights, but the law burdened adults who buy games for their children.
e: Rule: Brown (2011): violent imagery is protected; a content-based ban on selling violent games to minors gets strict scrutiny and fails.
oe: Correct. Following Stevens, legislatures can't add categories by balancing. Similar effects came from Bugs Bunny cartoons, and California conceded no direct causal link.
The Court held video games are speech, communicating ideas through characters, plot, music, and interaction.
Ginsberg adjusted an existing category (obscenity) for minors. California sought a wholly new category.
Minors are entitled to a significant measure of First Amendment protection; there is no "free-floating power" to restrict ideas children see.
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral speech — Violent imagery · Brown

q: According to the outline's governing principles for immoral speech, which statement is correct?
o: Government may restrict indecent speech anywhere children might encounter it, extending FCC v. Pacifica Foundation to all media.
Government may restrict any speech it reasonably finds immoral, as long as the restriction applies equally to adults and minors.
Protecting kids is always a compelling interest that satisfies strict scrutiny for any law aimed at minors.
Government almost never can restrict immoral speech to protect adults (obscenity aside), and it may protect kids only without blocking adult access.
e: Rule: Two overarching questions for immoral speech: who is the government protecting (adults or kids), and what harm is targeted (the content itself or an indirect harm)?
oe: Pacifica is a narrow broadcast exception. Bolger and the other cases refused to extend it.
Morality alone almost never justifies restricting speech to adults. Equal application doesn't cure that.
The interest is important, but laws still fail tailoring (Ashcroft II; Brown).
Correct. Offended adults are expected to look away, walk away, or toss out the mail; and kids have their own rights (Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association).
topic: Ch. 6 · Immoral speech — Immoral speech checklist · adults vs. kids

q: Why does the Court treat fraud as an unprotected category of speech?
o: Fraud is unprotected only when it is prosecuted criminally; civil fraud claims must satisfy actual malice.
History, plus demanding elements (knowing falsity, intent to mislead) that limit chilling.
Fraud causes emotional harm to its victims, and speech causing emotional harm is unprotected.
All false statements of fact are unprotected, and fraud is simply the most common kind of false statement.
e: Rule: Fraud is unprotected: historically excluded, and its demanding common-law elements (knowing falsity, materiality, intent to mislead) limit chilling.
oe: Fraud is unprotected whether pursued civilly or criminally. Actual malice is a defamation concept.
Correct. Fraud usually aims to obtain money or property. United States v. Hansen was fraud; United States v. Alvarez was not.
Emotional harm isn't the test (Snyder v. Phelps). Fraud's history and demanding elements are.
United States v. Alvarez rejected any general exception for false statements.
topic: Ch. 7 · Torts involving speech — Fraud

q: What must a public official prove to recover for defamation under New York Times v. Sullivan?
o: That the statement was false; the defendant must then prove it was reasonable.
That the defendant acted with ill will or a desire to harm the official, as "malice" means in ordinary English.
That the defendant was negligent in failing to verify the statement before publishing it.
Actual malice, meaning knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard of whether the statement was false.
e: Rule: Sullivan (1964): a public official can't recover for a defamatory falsehood about official conduct without proving actual malice (knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard).
oe: A rule requiring critics to guarantee truth, with only a truth defense, leads to self-censorship. That's what Sullivan rejected.
The Court defined "actual malice" as knowing or reckless falsity. Ill will is neither necessary nor sufficient.
Negligence is the Gertz floor for private plaintiffs on matters of public concern. Public officials must show actual malice.
Correct. Recklessness is enough; "malice" here doesn't mean ill will. The rule protects the "breathing space" free debate needs.
topic: Ch. 7 · Torts involving speech — Defamation · Sullivan

q: A private person sues over a false statement on a matter of public concern. Under Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc., what rules apply?
o: The plaintiff must prove actual malice for any recovery, just like a public official.
States may impose liability for at least negligence, but presumed or punitive damages require actual malice.
The plaintiff may recover only if the statement was made with ill will and caused provable economic loss.
States may impose strict liability, and presumed and punitive damages are available without any showing of fault.
e: Rule: Gertz (1974): private plaintiff, public concern: at least negligence for liability; actual malice for presumed or punitive damages.
oe: Gertz gave private plaintiffs a lower bar. Actual malice is needed only for presumed or punitive damages.
Correct. States may not impose liability without fault. Juries' uncontrolled discretion to award damages without proven loss compounds chilling.
Neither ill will nor economic loss is the Gertz standard. Negligence is the floor for liability.
Gertz forbade liability without fault on matters of public concern. Dun & Bradstreet relaxed the damages rule only for private-concern speech.
topic: Ch. 7 · Torts involving speech — Defamation · Gertz

q: What reasons did Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc. give for protecting private plaintiffs more than public officials and public figures?
o: False statements about private people are more likely to be intentional lies than errors.
Public officials can sue in federal court while private people must sue in state court, so states need more latitude.
Private people have less access to the media to rebut lies, and they haven't voluntarily exposed themselves to public scrutiny.
Private people's speech is less valuable, so statements about them deserve less constitutional protection.
e: Rule: Public officials and figures have greater access to channels of rebuttal and have voluntarily assumed the risk of scrutiny; private individuals are more vulnerable and more deserving of recovery.
oe: Gertz didn't rest on any such assumption. Its reasons were access to media and voluntary exposure.
Forum wasn't part of the reasoning. The reasons were self-help and voluntary assumption of risk.
Correct. Self-help (rebuttal) is the first remedy, and public figures invite attention. A private person "has relinquished no part of his interest in the protection of his own good name."
Gertz focused on the plaintiff's vulnerability and choices, not the value of private people's own speech.
topic: Ch. 7 · Torts involving speech — Why private plaintiffs differ

q: A credit agency falsely reports to a contractor's creditors that the contractor is insolvent. Under Dun & Bradstreet v. Greenmoss Builders (plurality), what follows?
o: Because the speech concerned a purely private matter, presumed and punitive damages are available without actual malice.
The plaintiff must prove negligence for liability and actual malice for presumed or punitive damages, exactly as in Gertz.
Because the plaintiff is a business, it is treated as a public figure and must prove actual malice.
The plaintiff can't recover at all, because credit reports are protected commercial speech.
e: Rule: Dun & Bradstreet (1985): private plaintiff, private concern: presumed and punitive damages without actual malice; the mens rea floor (negligence or strict liability) remains undecided.
oe: Correct. Speech on matters of public concern is at the heart of the First Amendment; purely private speech gets less stringent protection.
That's the Gertz rule for public-concern speech. Dun & Bradstreet held it doesn't apply to purely private matters.
The contractor was treated as an ordinary private plaintiff, not a public figure.
The Court allowed recovery. Whether strict liability is permitted remains an open question.
topic: Ch. 7 · Torts involving speech — Defamation · Dun & Bradstreet

q: In his dissent from the denial of certiorari in Berisha v. Lawson, why did Justice Gorsuch urge the Court to revisit New York Times v. Sullivan?
o: Actual malice is too easy to prove, so public officials win too many defamation suits against the press.
A majority of the Court had already voted to overrule Sullivan, and the cert denial was only a procedural delay.
Sullivan gave the press greater rights than ordinary individuals, which violates equal protection.
The changed media landscape may have turned Sullivan into a subsidy for spreading falsehoods.
e: Rule: Sullivan remains good law; Justices Thomas and Gorsuch have urged reconsidering it in light of the changed media landscape.
oe: Gorsuch's concern was the opposite: the standard is so hard to meet that falsehoods go unremedied.
The Court denied cert without explanation. Only Thomas and Gorsuch wrote to reconsider Sullivan.
The Court's doctrine doesn't give the press greater rights than individuals. That wasn't Gorsuch's argument.
Correct. Gorsuch argued that at the founding the press could be held liable in tort for getting facts wrong; Sullivan has become "an ironclad subsidy" for falsehood.
topic: Ch. 7 · Torts involving speech — Reconsidering Sullivan · Berisha

q: Which statement reflects the First Amendment limits on intentional infliction of emotional distress (IIED) claims?
o: A public figure can recover for IIED whenever a parody is so offensive that a jury finds it outrageous.
"Outrageousness" is too malleable a standard to impose liability for speech on public matters (Hustler Magazine v. Falwell; Snyder v. Phelps).
A private plaintiff can always recover for IIED, because Gertz lets states set their own standards for private plaintiffs.
IIED claims based on speech are barred entirely, because the tort is too new to fall within a historical exception.
e: Rule: Hustler (1988): public figures need a false statement of fact made with actual malice. Snyder (2011): speech on public concern in a public place can't be the basis for IIED liability because it's outrageous.
oe: Hustler reversed exactly that kind of verdict. The obvious parody couldn't reasonably be read as stating facts.
Correct. Hustler requires public figures to show a false statement of fact made with actual malice; Snyder protects speech on public concern in a public place.
Snyder v. Phelps barred recovery by a private plaintiff (a grieving father) because the speech concerned public matters.
The First Amendment limits IIED claims but doesn't bar them entirely. Speech on purely private matters may still support liability.
topic: Ch. 7 · Torts involving speech — IIED · Hustler and Snyder

q: In Snyder v. Phelps, the plaintiff was a private person, a grieving father. Why did the Court still rule for the Westboro Baptist Church?
o: The picketing occurred far enough from the funeral to be a valid time, place, and manner regulation.
The father was treated as a public figure because his son was a soldier killed in a war of public interest.
It focused on the speech's public-concern content and its public, peaceful setting, not on who sued.
The church's signs were religious expression protected by the Free Exercise Clause from tort liability.
e: Rule: Snyder (2011): whether speech is protected from IIED liability turns largely on whether it is of public or private concern, judged by all the circumstances.
oe: Snyder involved tort liability, not a TPM regulation, though the location mattered to whether the speech was protected.
The Court didn't reclassify the father as a public figure. Its focus was the speech's content and setting.
Correct. The distress came from the message. Parishioners holding "God Bless America" signs at the same spot wouldn't have been liable.
The Court decided the case under the Free Speech Clause based on public concern, not Free Exercise.
topic: Ch. 7 · Torts involving speech — Snyder · focus on content

q: Which statement about disclosing true information or appropriating a likeness is correct?
o: Lawfully obtained truthful news is protected, but airing a performer's entire act isn't (Zacchini).
A broadcaster may be held liable for airing an illegally intercepted call even if a third party made the recording.
Truthful information is unprotected whenever it invades someone's privacy, regardless of how it was obtained.
Media may broadcast any performance that is newsworthy, so Zacchini lost his right-of-publicity claim.
e: Rule: Truthful, lawfully obtained information on public matters is strongly protected (Florida Star; Bartnicki); right-of-publicity claims for a performer's entire act are not barred (Zacchini).
oe: Correct. Florida Star v. B.J.F. applied strict scrutiny to a damages award for lawfully obtained truthful information. Zacchini v. Scripps-Howard let the "human cannonball" recover because airing his entire act took its economic value.
Bartnicki held the media organization couldn't be liable where a third party did the interception and the matter was of public concern.
Truthful information is protected, at least where it was obtained lawfully (Florida Star; Bartnicki v. Vopper).
Zacchini won. The First Amendment doesn't immunize broadcasting a performer's entire act without consent.
topic: Ch. 7 · Torts involving speech — Truthful information and IP · Florida Star; Zacchini

q: Which of these is not commercial speech under the outline's definition?
o: A charity's mailing asking for donations to fund disaster relief.
A law firm's ad stating that it handles personal injury cases on contingency.
A nonprofit hospital's billboard advertising its new cardiac surgery center.
A sneaker company's social media post announcing a 20% discount on running shoes.
e: Rule: Commercial speech is speech that proposes a commercial transaction (selling goods or services); charitable solicitations are not commercial speech.
oe: Correct. Commercial speech is speech used to try to sell goods or services. Charitable solicitations (fundraising) aren't commercial speech.
Lawyer advertising is commercial speech with a measure of protection (Bates; Zauderer).
Nonprofits can engage in commercial speech. A hospital advertising its services is commercial speech.
An ad proposing a sale of goods at a price is classic commercial speech.
topic: Ch. 8 · Commercial speech — Commercial speech · definition

q: What did Virginia Pharmacy Board v. Virginia Citizens Consumer Council hold, and whose rights did it recognize?
o: Only the pharmacists could sue, because listeners have no rights of their own.
